> Glance is a small controller board for DIY heads-up glasses that display short lines of text in the wearer's line of sight, aimed at reading help and quick information like definitions or notes. A tiny OLED mounted on the frame reflects off a beam splitter angled toward the eye, so the text appears over the real world without blocking it.

**1.5h**

I started this session by getting started with the most basic components I would need for this project. This included an ESP32, OLED screen, and LED, a resistor, and two push buttons. I did this to primarily test the wiring logic between the parts. Now that I've confirmed this and that the code works on a Wokwi simulation, I'm going to move on to KiCad, to design the actual PCB for this project. The KiCad design will include the majority of the more complex components, that weren't integrated into the Wokwi sim. Lastly, this step also included setting up the repo, connecting it to Github, and setting up the necessary folders.

Set up KiCad and drew the schematic for my AR glasses PCB. It covers USB-C power, a battery charger, a 3.3V regulator, the ESP32 chip, an OLED display connector, two buttons and a debug LED.

Problem: I had placed a dev board symbol for the ESP32 (ESP32-C3-DevKitM-1), but my design uses the bare ESP32-C3-MINI-1 module. I installed Espressif’s library in KiCad, swapped in the correct symbol, and rewired it. The ESP32 errors cleared.

Status: Two small ERC errors left to fix (an unannotated resistor and a missing power flag).

AI use: Claude helped with KiCad steps and design review. I drew the schematic myself. No AI-written code.

Next: Fix the ERC errors, then assign footprints so I can turn the schematic into a PCB layout.

### 2026-10-10 – Talked with my dad and changed the project. GLANCE is now glasses for people who see fine at medium distance but need reading glasses up close. The idea is that the glasses figure out how far away you

**4h**

Talked with my dad and changed the project. GLANCE is now glasses for people who see fine at medium distance but need reading glasses up close. The idea is that the glasses figure out how far away you’re looking and adjust the lens power to match, instead of you switching between two pairs. (this change is not only due to wanting to solve an issue that my dad has, but also due to the complexity of the AR smart glasses I had orginally planned).

The hard part is knowing what distance you’re focused on, and that’s why the board suddenly has sensors. Two things tell you the distance. The first is a time-of-flight distance sensor facing outward, which measures how far the object in front of you is. The second is eye convergence: when you look at something close, both eyes rotate inward, and the angle between them tells you how far away your focus is. That’s the most accurate at reading distance, which is exactly the range that matters here. To measure each eye’s angle without cameras, I’m using an IR LED and two IR phototransistors per eye. The sclera (white) and the iris reflect IR differently, so the signal changes as the eye moves. Comparing the left and right readings gives the convergence angle. An ADS1115 ADC reads those four analog signals over I2C.

I chose IR sensors over cameras because the ESP32-S3 has only one camera port, so two eye cameras won’t fit, and photodiode sensing is much cheaper and smaller. I also added an IMU, so head tilt can be told apart from eye movement. The board has a header for the future lens driver, but the lens physics isn’t solved yet.

Tonight I swapped the ESP32-C3 for an ESP32-S3, drew the eye sensor circuits, and added headers for the distance sensor, IMU, lens output and serial debug. I also cleaned up my project folders into one GLANCE folder with board1 and board2, so board 1 stays safe. ERC came back with zero errors after I fixed a typo in a net label and a wrong footprint name.

The eye tracking is untested, so whether the sensors are accurate enough is an experiment for week 6. Next: assign footprints, update the PCB, place parts, and route.

### 2026-10-11 – Finished the PCB layout for Board 2, the ESP32-S3 sensing platform for the autofocal reading glasses. Placed all parts and hand-routed the USB pair and the main battery-to-3.3V power path. Locked thos

**5h**

Finished the PCB layout for Board 2, the ESP32-S3 sensing platform for the autofocal reading glasses. Placed all parts and hand-routed the USB pair and the main battery-to-3.3V power path. Locked those tracks, then autorouted the rest with Freerouting, which scored 990/1000 with 31 vias. Set up power net classes and filled GND planes on both layers. Worked the DRC down to zero real errors by fixing track widths, edge clearance and thermal vias, and by cleaning up dangling vias. Built the BOM on LCSC. Replaced the discontinued PT333-3B phototransistor with the PT334-6B. Exported the Gerbers and got a JLCPCB quote for the bare boards. Cut the funded BOM to fit the $30 tier, with the rest self-funded.
